subject: Constraints on a user defined function don't work

messages.author: 0bfa94c1afe543dd
messages.subject: Constraints on a user defined function don't work
parts:
Hi all,

I'm fitting a frontier estimation model in stan. The problem is that the estimated coefficients are at odds with the constraints that I put in the likelihood function even though all chains are well mixed. I didn't have this problem when I ran my code using a simple Metropolis-Hasting algorithm that I set up in R. It seems like that I made some inadvertent errors in writing up the rstan code. I looked up the manual several times but couldn't find what the problem is in my code. Could you anyone take a quick look at my script and let me know if I make any mistakes? 

My model is the following. There are two (negative) half quadratic functions as frontiers; a_1x^2 + b_1x +c_1 and a_2x^2 + b_2x +c_2. The likelihood function, "dist", is the distance of each data point (\chi, \gamma) from the corresponding frontier represented by (\chi_f, \gamma_f) (The distance is calculated using some baseline economic theory). Since the farther the data point is, the less likely, I used the exponential function with a parameter \delta. In my model, frontiers should envelop all the data points so there are no points outside the frontier. Therefore, I put some constraints in the likelihood as follows. 1. If the data points are outside the inner frontier but are inside the outer frontier, it calculates the distance from the outer frontier. 2. If the data points are inside the outer and inner frontier, it calculates the distance from the inner frontier. Otherwise, that is, the data points are outside the outer frontier, the distance is recored 10000, whose probability is almost zero in the exponential pdf with \delta around 2. (There are couple of other constraints other than these) From this model set-up, I should expect that the resulting coefficients and the generated frontiers don't have any data points inside the frontier, which is not the case in my result. The following is my code. Any comments will be much appreciated. 

Thanks!

functions {
  real dist(real chi_f_1, real chi_f_2, real chi, real gamma_f_1,  real gamma_f_2, real gamma, real w, real a_1, real b_1, real c_1, real a_2, real b_2, real c_2) {
    real dist;
    if(a_2*chi^2 + b_2*chi + c_2 <= gamma && a_1*chi^2 + b_1*chi + c_1 >= gamma && 2*a_1*chi + b_1 <= 0 && (1-w)*chi_f_1 + w* gamma_f_1 - (1-w)*chi - w* gamma >= 0){
      dist  = (1-w)*chi_f_1 + w* gamma_f_1 - (1-w)*chi - w* gamma ;
    } else if(a_1*chi^2 + b_1*chi + c_1 >= gamma && a_2*chi^2 + b_2*chi + c_2 > gamma && 2*a_2*chi + b_2 <= 0 && (1-w)*chi_f_2 + w* gamma_f_2 - (1-w)*chi - w* gamma >= 0) {
      dist =(1-w)*chi_f_2 + w* gamma_f_2 - (1-w)*chi - w* gamma ;
    } else {
      dist = 10000;
    }
    return (dist);
  }
}
data{
  int N;
  real chi[N];
  real gamma[N];
  real w[N];
}
parameters{
  real<upper = 0> a_1;
  real<upper = 0> b_1;
  real<lower = 0> c_1;
  real<upper = 0> a_2;
  real<upper = 0> b_2;
  real<lower = 0> c_2;
  real<lower = 0> delta;  
}
transformed parameters{
  real chi_f_1[N];
  real gamma_f_1[N];
  real chi_f_2[N];
  real gamma_f_2[N];

  
  for(i in 1:N){
    chi_f_1[i] = 1/2*(-(1-w[i])/w[i] - b_1)/a_1;
    gamma_f_1[i] = a_1*(1/2*(-(1-w[i])/w[i] - b_1)/a_1)^2 + b_1*(1/2*(-(1-w[i])/w[i] - b_1)/a_1) + c_1;
    chi_f_2[i] = 1/2*(-(1-w[i])/w[i] - b_2)/a_2;
    gamma_f_2[i] = a_2*( 1/2*(-(1-w[i])/w[i] - b_2)/a_2)^2 + b_2*(1/2*(-(1-w[i])/w[i] - b_2)/a_2) + c_2;
  }
  

}
model{
  real ps[N];
  a_1 ~ normal(-0.1, 0.1); 
  b_1 ~ normal(-1,0.5);
  c_1 ~ normal(5, 1);
  a_2 ~ normal(-0.1, 0.1); 
  b_2 ~ normal(-1, 0.5);
  c_2 ~ normal(2, 1);
  delta ~ normal(1,1);
  
    for(i in 1:N){
    ps[i] = exponential_lpdf(dist(chi_f_1[i], chi_f_2[i], chi[i], gamma_f_1[i], gamma_f_2[i], gamma[i], w[i],  a_1,  b_1,  c_1, a_2,  b_2,  c_2) | delta);
  }
  
  target += log_sum_exp(ps);
}
generated quantities {
  vector[N] gamma_sim_1;
  vector[N] gamma_sim_2;
  for(n in 1:N){
    gamma_sim_1[n] = a_1*chi[n]^2 + b_1*chi[n] + c_1;
    gamma_sim_2[n] = a_2*chi[n]^2 + b_2*chi[n] + c_2;
  }
}

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Constraints on a user defined function don't work
parts:
I don't know those models, but had two comments:

Stan uses the scale parameterization of normals---did you
really want normal priors with sd of 0.1?

> for(i in 1:N){
> ps[i] = exponential_lpdf(dist(chi_f_1[i], chi_f_2[i], chi[i], gamma_f_1[i], gamma_f_2[i], gamma[i], w[i], a_1, b_1, c_1, a_2, b_2, c_2) | delta);
> }
>
> target += log_sum_exp(ps);

If you put a distribution on a function of parameters, you need
to include the Jacobian adjustment.

Plus, I'm guessing you don't really want log_sum_exp here,
which gives you the log of the sum of the pdfs---you probably
want a product.

- Bob

Thank you so much for your kind comments. I really appreciate it. 

It seems like there are so many things I need to learn before I start coding this model up in stan. If you don't mind, could you elaborate on your comments a little bit. First, ps is basically my log-likelihood function. I thought the sampling should be done from the log-posterior, which is basically the sum of log-likelihood (with the prior). By "product", you mean the product of log likelihood function? Then, should it be target += prod(ps)? Second, could you elaborate on what you meant by "function of parameters?" Finally, I thought that a_1 ~ Normal(-0.1,0.1) says that the prior on a_1 is a normal with mean -0.1 and sd 0.1. Am I missing something here? 

Many thanks in advance! 

Jangho

First, ps is basically my log-likelihood function. I thought the sampling should be done from the log-posterior, which is basically the sum of log-likelihood (with the prior).

Exactly. So I think you want

target += sum(ps);

So those ps aren't densities, but log densities because
they're defined with the _lpdf (log pdf).

log_sum_exp(ps) = log SUM_n exp(ps[n])

whereas I think you want you want

sum(ps) = SUM_n ps[n]
> By "product", you mean the product of log likelihood function? Then, should it be target += prod(ps)? Second, could you elaborate on what you meant by "function of parameters?"

Check out the user manual chapter on Reparameterization
and Change of Variables to see where and why you need
a Jacobian.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Constraints on a user defined function don't work
parts:
Thanks a lob, Bob. 

Yes, sum(ps) = SUM_n ps[n] is exactly what I was looking for. 

About the Jacobian adjustment, I'll take a look at the relevant chapter you mentioned. Looks kind of tricky because I have 7 parameters. Will try it out, though. 

Thanks again for the comments!

Best,
On Tue, Oct 18, 2016 at 8:49 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

> On Oct 18, 2016, at 7:32 PM, Jangho Yang <yangj...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Thank you so much for your kind comments. I really appreciate it.
>
> It seems like there are so many things I need to learn before I start coding this model up in stan. If you don't mind, could you elaborate on your comments a little bit. First, ps is basically my log-likelihood function. I thought the sampling should be done from the log-posterior, which is basically the sum of log-likelihood (with the prior).

Exactly.  So I think you want

  target += sum(ps);

So those ps aren't densities, but log densities because
they're defined with the _lpdf (log pdf).

  log_sum_exp(ps) = log SUM_n exp(ps[n])

whereas I think you want you want

  sum(ps) = SUM_n ps[n]

> By "product", you mean the product of log likelihood function? Then, should it be target += prod(ps)? Second, could you elaborate on what you meant by "function of parameters?"

Check out the user manual chapter on Reparameterization
and Change of Variables to see where and why you need
a Jacobian.

> Finally, I thought that a_1 ~ Normal(-0.1,0.1) says that the prior on a_1 is a normal with mean -0.1 and sd 0.1. Am I missing something here?
>
> Many thanks in advance!
>
> Jangho
>
> On Tue, Oct 18, 2016 at 6:14 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> I don't know those models, but had two comments:
>
> Stan uses the scale parameterization of normals---did you
> really want normal priors with sd of 0.1?
>
> >  for(i in 1:N){
> >     ps[i] = exponential_lpdf(dist(chi_f_1[i], chi_f_2[i], chi[i], gamma_f_1[i], gamma_f_2[i], gamma[i], w[i],  a_1,  b_1,  c_1, a_2,  b_2,  c_2) | delta);
> >   }
> >
> >   target += log_sum_exp(ps);
>
> If you put a distribution on a function of parameters, you need
> to include the Jacobian adjustment.
>
> Plus, I'm guessing you don't really want log_sum_exp here,
> which gives you the log of the sum of the pdfs---you probably
> want a product.
>
> - Bob
>
> > On Oct 17, 2016, at 6:50 PM, Jangho Yang <yangj...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Hi all,
> >
> > I'm fitting a frontier estimation model in stan. The problem is that the estimated coefficients are at odds with the constraints that I put in the likelihood function even though all chains are well mixed. I didn't have this problem when I ran my code using a simple Metropolis-Hasting algorithm that I set up in R. It seems like that I made some inadvertent errors in writing up the rstan code. I looked up the manual several times but couldn't find what the problem is in my code. Could you anyone take a quick look at my script and let me know if I make any mistakes?
> >
> > My model is the following. There are two (negative) half quadratic functions as frontiers; a_1x^2 + b_1x +c_1 and a_2x^2 + b_2x +c_2. The likelihood function, "dist", is the distance of each data point (\chi, \gamma) from the corresponding frontier represented by (\chi_f, \gamma_f) (The distance is calculated using some baseline economic theory). Since the farther the data point is, the less likely, I used the exponential function with a parameter \delta. In my model, frontiers should envelop all the data points so there are no points outside the frontier. Therefore, I put some constraints in the likelihood as follows. 1. If the data points are outside the inner frontier but are inside the outer frontier, it calculates the distance from the outer frontier. 2. If the data points are inside the outer and inner frontier, it calculates the distance from the inner frontier. Otherwise, that is, the data points are outside the outer frontier, the distance is recored 10000, whose probability is almost zero in the exponential pdf with \delta around 2. (There are couple of other constraints other than these) From this model set-up, I should expect that the resulting coefficients and the generated frontiers don't have any data points inside the frontier, which is not the case in my result. The following is my code. Any comments will be much appreciated.
> >
> > Thanks!
> >
> > functions {
> >   real dist(real chi_f_1, real chi_f_2, real chi, real gamma_f_1,  real gamma_f_2, real gamma, real w, real a_1, real b_1, real c_1, real a_2, real b_2, real c_2) {
> >     real dist;
> >     if(a_2*chi^2 + b_2*chi + c_2 <= gamma && a_1*chi^2 + b_1*chi + c_1 >= gamma && 2*a_1*chi + b_1 <= 0 && (1-w)*chi_f_1 + w* gamma_f_1 - (1-w)*chi - w* gamma >= 0){
> >       dist  = (1-w)*chi_f_1 + w* gamma_f_1 - (1-w)*chi - w* gamma ;
> >     } else if(a_1*chi^2 + b_1*chi + c_1 >= gamma && a_2*chi^2 + b_2*chi + c_2 > gamma && 2*a_2*chi + b_2 <= 0 && (1-w)*chi_f_2 + w* gamma_f_2 - (1-w)*chi - w* gamma >= 0) {
> >       dist =(1-w)*chi_f_2 + w* gamma_f_2 - (1-w)*chi - w* gamma ;
> >     } else {
> >       dist = 10000;
> >     }
> >     return (dist);
> >   }
> > }
> > data{
> >   int N;
> >   real chi[N];
> >   real gamma[N];
> >   real w[N];
> > }
> > parameters{
> >   real<upper = 0> a_1;
> >   real<upper = 0> b_1;
> >   real<lower = 0> c_1;
> >   real<upper = 0> a_2;
> >   real<upper = 0> b_2;
> >   real<lower = 0> c_2;
> >   real<lower = 0> delta;
> > }
> > transformed parameters{
> >   real chi_f_1[N];
> >   real gamma_f_1[N];
> >   real chi_f_2[N];
> >   real gamma_f_2[N];
> >
> >
> >   for(i in 1:N){
> >     chi_f_1[i] = 1/2*(-(1-w[i])/w[i] - b_1)/a_1;
> >     gamma_f_1[i] = a_1*(1/2*(-(1-w[i])/w[i] - b_1)/a_1)^2 + b_1*(1/2*(-(1-w[i])/w[i] - b_1)/a_1) + c_1;
> >     chi_f_2[i] = 1/2*(-(1-w[i])/w[i] - b_2)/a_2;
> >     gamma_f_2[i] = a_2*( 1/2*(-(1-w[i])/w[i] - b_2)/a_2)^2 + b_2*(1/2*(-(1-w[i])/w[i] - b_2)/a_2) + c_2;
> >   }
> >
> >
> > }
> > model{
> >   real ps[N];
> >   a_1 ~ normal(-0.1, 0.1);
> >   b_1 ~ normal(-1,0.5);
> >   c_1 ~ normal(5, 1);
> >   a_2 ~ normal(-0.1, 0.1);
> >   b_2 ~ normal(-1, 0.5);
> >   c_2 ~ normal(2, 1);
> >   delta ~ normal(1,1);
> >
> >     for(i in 1:N){
> >     ps[i] = exponential_lpdf(dist(chi_f_1[i], chi_f_2[i], chi[i], gamma_f_1[i], gamma_f_2[i], gamma[i], w[i],  a_1,  b_1,  c_1, a_2,  b_2,  c_2) | delta);
> >   }
> >
> >   target += log_sum_exp(ps);
> > }
> > generated quantities {
> >   vector[N] gamma_sim_1;
> >   vector[N] gamma_sim_2;
> >   for(n in 1:N){
> >     gamma_sim_1[n] = a_1*chi[n]^2 + b_1*chi[n] + c_1;
> >     gamma_sim_2[n] = a_2*chi[n]^2 + b_2*chi[n] + c_2;
> >   }
> > }
> >
> >
> >
> >
> >
> >

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Constraints on a user defined function don't work
parts:
Yes. Stan has a determinant function, but hopefully it
won't come to that---often the Jacobian is diagonal, triangular,
or blocked, which makes the determinant calc much easier.

Or you can think about the model differently and put priors
on the basic quantities directly. We usually do that rather than
trying to put distributions on complex transforms of parameters,
mainly because it's usually much easier to understand generatively.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Constraints on a user defined function don't work
parts: You're right. Making a different model might be better in this case. Thanks again!
On Wed, Oct 19, 2016 at 11:33 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

Yes.  Stan has a determinant function, but hopefully it
won't come to that---often the Jacobian is diagonal, triangular,
or blocked, which makes the determinant calc much easier.

Or you can think about the model differently and put priors
on the basic quantities directly.  We usually do that rather than
trying to put distributions on complex transforms of parameters,
mainly because it's usually much easier to understand generatively.

- Bob

> On Oct 19, 2016, at 11:26 AM, Jangho Yang <yangj...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Thanks a lob, Bob.
>
> Yes, sum(ps) = SUM_n ps[n] is exactly what I was looking for.
>
> About the Jacobian adjustment, I'll take a look at the relevant chapter you mentioned. Looks kind of tricky because I have 7 parameters. Will try it out, though.
>
> Thanks again for the comments!
>
> Best,
>
>
> On Tue, Oct 18, 2016 at 8:49 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>
> > On Oct 18, 2016, at 7:32 PM, Jangho Yang <yangj...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Thank you so much for your kind comments. I really appreciate it.
> >
> > It seems like there are so many things I need to learn before I start coding this model up in stan. If you don't mind, could you elaborate on your comments a little bit. First, ps is basically my log-likelihood function. I thought the sampling should be done from the log-posterior, which is basically the sum of log-likelihood (with the prior).
>
> Exactly.  So I think you want
>
>   target += sum(ps);
>
> So those ps aren't densities, but log densities because
> they're defined with the _lpdf (log pdf).
>
>   log_sum_exp(ps) = log SUM_n exp(ps[n])
>
> whereas I think you want you want
>
>   sum(ps) = SUM_n ps[n]
>
> > By "product", you mean the product of log likelihood function? Then, should it be target += prod(ps)? Second, could you elaborate on what you meant by "function of parameters?"
>
> Check out the user manual chapter on Reparameterization
> and Change of Variables to see where and why you need
> a Jacobian.
>
> > Finally, I thought that a_1 ~ Normal(-0.1,0.1) says that the prior on a_1 is a normal with mean -0.1 and sd 0.1. Am I missing something here?
> >
> > Many thanks in advance!
> >
> > Jangho
> >
> > On Tue, Oct 18, 2016 at 6:14 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> > I don't know those models, but had two comments:
> >
> > Stan uses the scale parameterization of normals---did you
> > really want normal priors with sd of 0.1?
> >
> > >  for(i in 1:N){
> > >     ps[i] = exponential_lpdf(dist(chi_f_1[i], chi_f_2[i], chi[i], gamma_f_1[i], gamma_f_2[i], gamma[i], w[i],  a_1,  b_1,  c_1, a_2,  b_2,  c_2) | delta);
> > >   }
> > >
> > >   target += log_sum_exp(ps);
> >
> > If you put a distribution on a function of parameters, you need
> > to include the Jacobian adjustment.
> >
> > Plus, I'm guessing you don't really want log_sum_exp here,
> > which gives you the log of the sum of the pdfs---you probably
> > want a product.
> >
> > - Bob
> >
> > > On Oct 17, 2016, at 6:50 PM, Jangho Yang <yangj...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > >
> > > Hi all,
> > >
> > > I'm fitting a frontier estimation model in stan. The problem is that the estimated coefficients are at odds with the constraints that I put in the likelihood function even though all chains are well mixed. I didn't have this problem when I ran my code using a simple Metropolis-Hasting algorithm that I set up in R. It seems like that I made some inadvertent errors in writing up the rstan code. I looked up the manual several times but couldn't find what the problem is in my code. Could you anyone take a quick look at my script and let me know if I make any mistakes?
> > >
> > > My model is the following. There are two (negative) half quadratic functions as frontiers; a_1x^2 + b_1x +c_1 and a_2x^2 + b_2x +c_2. The likelihood function, "dist", is the distance of each data point (\chi, \gamma) from the corresponding frontier represented by (\chi_f, \gamma_f) (The distance is calculated using some baseline economic theory). Since the farther the data point is, the less likely, I used the exponential function with a parameter \delta. In my model, frontiers should envelop all the data points so there are no points outside the frontier. Therefore, I put some constraints in the likelihood as follows. 1. If the data points are outside the inner frontier but are inside the outer frontier, it calculates the distance from the outer frontier. 2. If the data points are inside the outer and inner frontier, it calculates the distance from the inner frontier. Otherwise, that is, the data points are outside the outer frontier, the distance is recored 10000, whose probability is almost zero in the exponential pdf with \delta around 2. (There are couple of other constraints other than these) From this model set-up, I should expect that the resulting coefficients and the generated frontiers don't have any data points inside the frontier, which is not the case in my result. The following is my code. Any comments will be much appreciated.
> > >
> > > Thanks!
> > >
> > > functions {
> > >   real dist(real chi_f_1, real chi_f_2, real chi, real gamma_f_1,  real gamma_f_2, real gamma, real w, real a_1, real b_1, real c_1, real a_2, real b_2, real c_2) {
> > >     real dist;
> > >     if(a_2*chi^2 + b_2*chi + c_2 <= gamma && a_1*chi^2 + b_1*chi + c_1 >= gamma && 2*a_1*chi + b_1 <= 0 && (1-w)*chi_f_1 + w* gamma_f_1 - (1-w)*chi - w* gamma >= 0){
> > >       dist  = (1-w)*chi_f_1 + w* gamma_f_1 - (1-w)*chi - w* gamma ;
> > >     } else if(a_1*chi^2 + b_1*chi + c_1 >= gamma && a_2*chi^2 + b_2*chi + c_2 > gamma && 2*a_2*chi + b_2 <= 0 && (1-w)*chi_f_2 + w* gamma_f_2 - (1-w)*chi - w* gamma >= 0) {
> > >       dist =(1-w)*chi_f_2 + w* gamma_f_2 - (1-w)*chi - w* gamma ;
> > >     } else {
> > >       dist = 10000;
> > >     }
> > >     return (dist);
> > >   }
> > > }
> > > data{
> > >   int N;
> > >   real chi[N];
> > >   real gamma[N];
> > >   real w[N];
> > > }
> > > parameters{
> > >   real<upper = 0> a_1;
> > >   real<upper = 0> b_1;
> > >   real<lower = 0> c_1;
> > >   real<upper = 0> a_2;
> > >   real<upper = 0> b_2;
> > >   real<lower = 0> c_2;
> > >   real<lower = 0> delta;
> > > }
> > > transformed parameters{
> > >   real chi_f_1[N];
> > >   real gamma_f_1[N];
> > >   real chi_f_2[N];
> > >   real gamma_f_2[N];
> > >
> > >
> > >   for(i in 1:N){
> > >     chi_f_1[i] = 1/2*(-(1-w[i])/w[i] - b_1)/a_1;
> > >     gamma_f_1[i] = a_1*(1/2*(-(1-w[i])/w[i] - b_1)/a_1)^2 + b_1*(1/2*(-(1-w[i])/w[i] - b_1)/a_1) + c_1;
> > >     chi_f_2[i] = 1/2*(-(1-w[i])/w[i] - b_2)/a_2;
> > >     gamma_f_2[i] = a_2*( 1/2*(-(1-w[i])/w[i] - b_2)/a_2)^2 + b_2*(1/2*(-(1-w[i])/w[i] - b_2)/a_2) + c_2;
> > >   }
> > >
> > >
> > > }
> > > model{
> > >   real ps[N];
> > >   a_1 ~ normal(-0.1, 0.1);
> > >   b_1 ~ normal(-1,0.5);
> > >   c_1 ~ normal(5, 1);
> > >   a_2 ~ normal(-0.1, 0.1);
> > >   b_2 ~ normal(-1, 0.5);
> > >   c_2 ~ normal(2, 1);
> > >   delta ~ normal(1,1);
> > >
> > >     for(i in 1:N){
> > >     ps[i] = exponential_lpdf(dist(chi_f_1[i], chi_f_2[i], chi[i], gamma_f_1[i], gamma_f_2[i], gamma[i], w[i],  a_1,  b_1,  c_1, a_2,  b_2,  c_2) | delta);
> > >   }
> > >
> > >   target += log_sum_exp(ps);
> > > }
> > > generated quantities {
> > >   vector[N] gamma_sim_1;
> > >   vector[N] gamma_sim_2;
> > >   for(n in 1:N){
> > >     gamma_sim_1[n] = a_1*chi[n]^2 + b_1*chi[n] + c_1;
> > >     gamma_sim_2[n] = a_2*chi[n]^2 + b_2*chi[n] + c_2;
> > >   }
> > > }
